newsitem.title: USA: Death toll from Michigan storm rises to eight.
newsitem.headline: Death toll from Michigan storm rises to eight.

text.p: The death toll from a series of tornadoes and thunderstorms in southeastern Michigan stood at eight on Thursday and police said it could go higher.

Five people from a summer picnic outing in Grosse Pointe Farms were killed Wednesday evening when the shelter they were under was picked up and swept into nearby Lake St. Clair. The dead included two adults and three children. Up to 12 people may have been injured.
At a mobile home park outside of Holly, northwest of Detroit, two people were killed when a tornado ripped apart several homes. In Flint, Michigan, one person was reported killed by a falling tree.
Detroit Mayor Dennis Archer and Michigan Gov. John Engler were scheduled to tour the city and give a report on the destruction from the storms, including some possible deaths in Detroit.
"I'm not sure there aren't any in the city," Officer Bill Ratliff said Thursday. He declined to give details until the mayor and governor's tour.

Through the night, Wayne County and Detroit Police used extra officers to keep order in the hardest hit areas, although there were some reports of looting. A state of emergency was declared on Wednesday night.
"It was pretty quiet, no major incidents other than the storm itself," Ratliff said.
Local utilities reported that more than 270,000 residents had lost power. Flooding continued to snarl traffic, and summer schools reported they would be closed for the day.

Swirling with winds of 60 to 100 mph (100 kph to 160 kph), the storms hit the area shortly before rush hour. They tore houses from foundations, sent trees through buildings, flipped cars, downed power lines and dumped up to 4 inches (10 cm) of rain, prompting flash flood warnings.

Two of the areas hardest hit were the Detroit communities of Highland Park and Hamtramck. Jeseca Woodard, 17, told Reuters she was upstairs in her Highland Park home when the lights starting blinking and high winds began blowing in the windows.
"I closed my eyes because I didn't want to get glass in them and when I opened my eyes, I looked up and I could see the sky," she said.
After realizing the roof had been blown off, Woodard, who was not injured, said she ran into the basement to wait out the storm with her mother.
"The attic was gone and everything," she said.
